Olympus. The sacred mountain dwelling of the twelve Olympian gods, standing as the cosmological center of Greek mythology. Located in northern Greece, this divine realm serves as the administrative and social heart of the pantheon, where gods feast, debate, and scheme over mortal affairs. For ancient Greeks, Olympus was both a physical place and a transcendent space beyond mortal reach.

The twelve major Olympian gods—including Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Aphrodite, Apollo, and Athena—reside on Olympus as a hierarchical community. Zeus rules as king of the gods from his throne atop the mountain, making executive decisions that bind all divine and mortal realms. The mountain is shrouded in perpetual cloud and mist, making it invisible to mortals. The gods feast on ambrosia and nectar, immortal foods that sustain their eternal existence.

Divine politics play out in Olympian assemblies, where gods propose quarrels, form alliances, and distribute divine favor to chosen heroes and champions on Earth. The mountain can shift location in different myths—sometimes northern Greece, sometimes imagined as a celestial realm beyond geographic space. Not all gods reside on Olympus; Hades rules the underworld and Poseidon dominates the sea, while minor deities occupy other sacred sites. Mortal heroes who earned divine favor were sometimes granted immortality and a place in Olympus, blurring the boundary between divine and human realms.
